segments: [p. 2] For a space of eighty years, this aim has not been contemplated by any of our people,
and no one of our sort has ventured to undertake it —
that is to say, since the time of the blessed elder, the late Patriarch Mor Michael, who composed that great three-part chronicle,
and who brought back to life, in his own work, what had grown old and worn away from the chronicles of Eusebius — I mean the one of Caesarea —
and of Socrates the Scholastic,
and of Zacharias Rhetor {OCR?},
and of John of Asia,
and of Dionysius of Tel Mahre —
he revived in that work of his.
A breach which resembles [destruction] and a sudden ruin that is invited seemed to me to be happening among us and in our nation,
when notable events — both secular and ecclesiastical — which occurred in the period before us
and in these our own times, should be forgotten and not be found,
when after a long lapse of time they might be sought for.
Therefore, when the opportunity arose to visit the library of the city of Maragheh in Azerbaijan,
I gathered into this small composition of mine, from many volumes — Syriac, Arabic, and Persian — right there, accounts worthy of remembrance.
And secular rule I brought down from the patriarchs, the first of whom was Adam,
and from them to the judges of the Hebrews,
then to their kings,
then to the Chaldeans,
then to the Medes,
then to the Persians,
then to the pagan Greeks,
then to the Romans,
then to the Christian Greeks,
then to the Arabs,
then to the Huns of our days, in order, one after another, I completed [it].
And while I concluded these in the first part of the Chronography,
in ecclesiastical matters I began from Aaron, the first high priest,
and with those who stand at the head today, I completed the second part, which is the Ecclesiastical [History].
This part I also sealed in two discourses:
the first discourse concerning that Western high priesthood of Antioch,
and the second discourse concerning this Eastern one of ours.
